subject: biology
title: Water and inorganic ions
key_idea: Water molecules are polar, so they form hydrogen bonds with each other. These bonds give water the properties that suit it to life: it is a solvent, a metabolite, a coolant and a stable habitat. Inorganic ions dissolved in cells and fluids each have a specific role.

blocks.text: Water is a small molecule with an uneven spread of charge. This section covers why that makes water cohesive.

items.meaning: A molecule with a slightly negative end and a slightly positive end.
A molecule that is a dipole, so it attracts other charged and polar particles.
A weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen atom and a slightly negative atom on another molecule.

items: In H₂O the oxygen atom pulls the shared electrons towards itself.
Oxygen is slightly negative (δ−) and each hydrogen is slightly positive (δ+).
The δ+ hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the δ− oxygen of a neighbour: a **hydrogen bond**.
Each hydrogen bond is weak, but there are very many, so together they are strong.
Water is a dipole because oxygen is δ− and hydrogen is δ+.
Hydrogen bonds form between neighbouring water molecules.
Many weak bonds together give water its special properties.

sections.heading: Properties of water and their roles

blocks.text: Each property of water follows from its polarity and hydrogen bonding. This section links each property to a role in living organisms.

rows: Polar water molecules surround charged ions and polar molecules and pull them apart.
Metabolic reactions happen in solution in cytoplasm. Ions, glucose and amino acids are carried in blood, tissue fluid, xylem and phloem.
Water takes part in reactions as a reactant or a product.
Used in hydrolysis and photosynthesis. Released in condensation and respiration.
A lot of energy is needed to break hydrogen bonds and raise the temperature.
Buffers changes in temperature. Cells and body fluids stay stable, and lakes and seas make a stable habitat.
A lot of energy is needed to break the hydrogen bonds between molecules and evaporate water.
Sweating and transpiration cool an organism with little water lost.
Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules together.
Continuous columns of water are pulled up xylem. Surface tension lets small animals walk on water.

items: Water is the main component of cytoplasm and body fluids, so it is also the **transport medium** for dissolved substances.
Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats and insulates the water below it. Aquatic life survives under frozen ponds.

diagram.alt: A sorting activity. Roles of water are sorted by the property that explains them: solvent, heat properties or cohesion.
diagram.prompt: Sort each role of water into the property that explains it.

items.text: Carries glucose and ions in the blood
A pond changes temperature slowly, so it is a stable habitat
Pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem
Surface tension supports a pond skater

items: Solvent action allows reactions and transport in solution.
High specific heat capacity buffers temperature changes.
High latent heat of vaporisation gives a cooling effect.
Cohesion supports water columns and gives surface tension.

blocks.text: Inorganic ions are dissolved in cytoplasm and body fluids. Some are at high concentrations and some at very low concentrations.
Each type of ion has a specific role that depends on its properties and charge.

rows: Sets pH: more H⁺ means more acidic. Also builds up gradients across membranes.
Makes a solution alkaline. Together with H⁺ it sets pH.
Moves glucose and amino acids into cells by co-transport. Also needed for nerve impulses.
Needed for nerve impulses. Helps to open stomata.
Strengthens bones and teeth. Needed for muscle contraction and blood clotting.
Part of the haem group in haemoglobin, where oxygen binds.
Part of DNA, RNA and ATP, and of phospholipids.
Carries carbon dioxide in the blood. Helps to buffer pH.
Balances the charge of positive ions. Moves into red blood cells as HCO₃⁻ moves out (chloride shift).
Taken up by plants to make amino acids and nucleotides.
A source of nitrogen. Bacteria convert it to nitrate.

items: Each ion has a specific role set by its charge and properties.
H⁺ sets pH, Fe²⁺ is in haemoglobin, Na⁺ drives co-transport, PO₄³⁻ is in DNA and ATP.

checks.q: Explain how hydrogen bonds form between water molecules.
checks.a: Oxygen is slightly negative (δ−) and hydrogen is slightly positive (δ+) because water is polar. The δ+ hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the δ− oxygen of another, forming a hydrogen bond.

checks.q: Explain why sweating cools the body with little loss of water.
checks.a: Water has a high latent heat of vaporisation. A lot of heat energy is taken from the body to break the hydrogen bonds when sweat evaporates, so a small mass of water gives a large cooling effect.

checks.q: State two ways the properties of water help transport in the xylem of a plant.
checks.a: Cohesion between water molecules (hydrogen bonds) holds the water together as a continuous column. Water is a solvent, so it carries dissolved mineral ions.

items: Water keeps cells turgid, supports non-woody stems, and is a reactant in photosynthesis.
Water carries dissolved mineral ions from the roots in the xylem.
**Nitrate** is used to make amino acids, proteins and nucleotides. A shortage causes stunted growth and yellow older leaves.
**Calcium ions** form calcium pectate in the middle lamella between cell walls. A shortage causes poor growth of roots and shoots.
**Magnesium ions** are part of chlorophyll. A shortage causes yellow leaves (chlorosis), because less chlorophyll can be made.

blocks.text: Water in blood and tissue fluid

items: Water is the main component of blood plasma and tissue fluid.
As a solvent it carries glucose, amino acids, ions, urea and hormones in solution.
Its high specific heat capacity means blood carries heat around the body without large changes in its own temperature.
Heat from active organs is distributed evenly and lost at the skin.

blocks.text: Water as a habitat and coolant

items: Aquatic eukaryotes and prokaryotes live in water, which is a stable habitat because of its high specific heat capacity.
Ice floats, so water under it stays liquid and organisms survive the winter.
Evaporation of water from skin (sweat) or leaves (transpiration) is a coolant in eukaryotes.
Prokaryotes need water as a solvent: all metabolic reactions in their cytoplasm happen in solution.
